Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger for a life-threatening illness trauma unless there was a very specific exposure context; the other items point more toward nightmares/body sensations/illness-related reexperiencing, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other threat and memory items describe fear, bodily alarm, pain, sensory recall, and dysregulated emotion rather than impulsive or reckless responding, so this item stands out as clinically disconnected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: Global mistrust of other people is a weak fit with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness in the absence of any interpersonal betrayal, assault, or persecution content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the appraisals are centered on bodily threat and fear of losing control, making this item comparatively incoherent.

vignette:
Amir believed his hands were his most reliable asset. For fifteen years, they had been steady, creative, and sure, snipping and styling in his bustling salon, a place filled with the scent of shampoo and the easy chatter of his clients. That sense of reliability shattered nine months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. One moment he was laughing with a longtime customer, scissors in hand; the next, a crushing weight descended on his chest, a brutal, searing pain that stole his breath and sent a terrifying ache down his left arm. He remembers the metallic taste in his mouth, the smell of antiseptic on the paramedic’s gloves, and the disorienting blur of ceiling tiles as he was wheeled through the emergency room. He had survived a sudden, severe cardiac event that the doctors called a fluke for a man of 38. But while his heart had physically healed, his sense of safety had not.

In the weeks that followed, Amir tried to reclaim his old life, but it was as if the memory of the event had lodged itself in his body. At first, it was the nightmares, vivid and chaotic, that left him waking in a tangle of sweat-soaked sheets. Even when he couldn't recall the specifics of the dream, a residue of pure dread would cling to him all morning, making the simple act of getting out of bed feel monumental. Then came the phantom sensations. Standing at his station, the clean, sharp smell of a particular styling product would suddenly be replaced by the sterile, chemical scent of the ICU, a smell so real he would gag. With the scent came a ghostly echo of the pain, a hot clenching in his chest that would make him drop his comb and brace himself against the counter, convinced it was happening all over again. Sometimes, there was no trigger at all; just a sudden, overwhelming wave of horror that would rise in his throat while he was driving or making dinner, an intense emotion completely untethered to any image or thought.

These experiences became his secret shame. He was certain he was going crazy, that his mind had broken in some fundamental way. He began to see his own body as an enemy, a traitor that was constantly sounding a false alarm. He felt perpetually on edge, his shoulders tight and his jaw clenched, as if waiting for the next blow. A routine dental appointment a few months ago became an ordeal; the simple act of reclining in the chair and having a medical professional lean over him sent his heart into a frantic, hammering rhythm. He felt dizzy, his palms grew slick with sweat, and he had to pretend to have a coughing fit just to get them to stop. He never went back to have the filling completed. His mother, trying to be helpful, had put together a small album of photos from his time in the hospital, showing him surrounded by family. The sight of his own pale face, tubes taped to his skin, sent such a jolt of fear through him that he had to shove the book in a drawer, unable to look at it again.

The salon, once his sanctuary, was now a minefield. The constant physical tension made the long hours on his feet exhausting, and he found himself watching his own reflection in the mirror, scrutinizing his complexion, monitoring his breathing. He had come to believe that any strong emotion—even a flash of anger at a rude driver or a wave of sadness watching a film—was dangerous, a potential trigger for another attack. He began cancelling last-minute appointments, telling clients he wasn't feeling well, which was technically true. The loss of income was worrying, but the fear of collapsing in front of a client was worse. He felt utterly alone with this, convinced that he could no longer trust the very body he lived in. It was after a particularly bad panic attack during a routine blood pressure check at a pharmacy kiosk—an attack that left him breathless and shaking on a public bench—that Amir finally made a call to seek help. He didn't know if he could ever feel normal again, but he knew he could not continue to live as a prisoner in his own skin, perpetually waiting for a catastrophe that had already happened.
